title: US wind growth is becoming a race against the clock
gist: Wood Mackenzie's US Wind Energy Monitor Q2 2026 finds US wind splitting into a two-speed market: construction-ready projects are being rushed to beat production/investment tax-credit deadlines (Q1 2026 construction starts +8% YoY, firm turbine orders over 5x Q1 2025), while permitting delays push the early-stage pipeline out and shift the onshore new-build peak from 2027 to 2028. Beyond 2030 the author argues there is no cliff edge but a long readjustment, with ~81 GW of fleet aged 15+ years by 2035 making repowering the main growth vector on commercial rather than tax-equity logic.

insights.claim: US wind projects that began physical construction before July 4, 2026 have until as late as December 31, 2030 to be placed in service and still capture federal production or investment tax credits, giving safe-harboured projects a four-and-a-half-year execution runway.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Defines the hard window for equipment deliveries, EPC bookings and tax-equity demand; projects with a documented pre-July-2026 construction start carry materially lower policy risk than the rest of the pipeline.
insights.quote: Projects that began physical construction before July 4, 2026 must be placed in service, as late as December 31st, 2030, to secure tax credits.
insights.locator: The shift from pipeline growth to project execution

insights.claim: US wind projects that missed the July 2026 construction-start deadline must be fully operational by as late as December 31, 2027 to obtain federal tax credits, compressing permitting, offtake, financing and equipment procurement into a roughly 18-month sprint.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Any non-safe-harboured project without permits, grid connection and turbines already secured is effectively uneconomic on credits and should be discounted out of developer pipelines.
insights.quote: Those that missed the construction-start deadline must be fully operational as late as December 31, 2027 to obtain the credits.
insights.locator: Those that missed the construction-start deadline

insights.claim: In US wind, holding a position in the development pipeline no longer confers value by itself; only projects that can clear permitting, offtake, financing and equipment procurement fast enough to hit the tax-credit deadlines retain economic worth.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Argues for repricing developer pipelines by maturity stage rather than headline GW, and for a bid market in late-stage, permitted assets.
insights.quote: For developers, the message is straightforward: securing a position in the pipeline is no longer enough.
insights.locator: For developers, the message is straightforward

insights.claim: US wind construction starts rose 8% year-on-year in Q1 2026 while firm turbine orders exceeded more than five times the level recorded in Q1 2025, a surge Wood Mackenzie attributes to urgency around the closing tax-credit window rather than underlying demand growth.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Turbine manufacturers' near-term backlogs are inflated by a policy pull-forward; treat the 5x order jump as a one-off rather than a run-rate when modelling OEM revenue beyond the safe-harbour window.
insights.quote: Construction starts increased 8% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, while firm turbine orders exceeded more than five times the level recorded during the first quarter of 2025.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie raised its five-year US greenfield wind new-build forecast by 5% quarter-on-quarter and expects total annual US wind additions to peak in 2027, with offshore wind contributing to that peak.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Sets 2027 as the cyclical high-water mark for US wind capex and installation revenue; positions built for growth past that year need a repowering or non-subsidy thesis.
insights.quote: the five-year new build wind forecast for greenfield projects rising 5% quarter-on-quarter

insights.claim: The near-term strength in US wind construction comes at the cost of new project origination, because developers are prioritising execution of existing assets over planning new ones, making the current growth unlikely to be sustained.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Flags an air pocket in the early-stage pipeline that will show up as a post-peak drop in orders and EPC activity roughly three to five years out.
insights.quote: Yet this growth looks unlikely to be sustained, as developers prioritise execution over planning new projects.

insights.claim: US wind has split into a two-speed market in which projects holding permits, offtake and grid connection agreements are being accelerated into the remaining tax-credit window while less mature developments face a far more uncertain path, creating a growing valuation premium on project maturity.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: A usable screen for developer equities and asset acquisitions: sort pipelines by permit/offtake/interconnection status, not GW, and expect bifurcated pricing between the two buckets.
insights.quote: A two-speed market has been created, with a growing premium on project maturity.
insights.locator: When will onshore wind development peak?

insights.claim: Federal permitting delays are pushing less mature US wind projects further into the decade, moving the expected largest volume of new-build onshore wind capacity from 2027 to 2028.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: A one-year slip in the onshore peak shifts turbine delivery, installation and balance-of-plant revenue recognition into 2028 for OEMs and contractors.
insights.quote: As federal permitting delays push less mature projects further into the decade, the largest volume of new-build onshore capacity is now expected in 2028 rather than 2027.
insights.locator: When will onshore wind development peak?

insights.claim: Corporate PPA demand for US wind is strengthening on the back of data centre growth, with Google and Xcel Energy's 1.9 GW portfolio deal announced in Q1 2026 illustrating the scale of data-centre-driven procurement.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Gigawatt-scale hyperscaler PPAs are becoming the marginal buyer of US wind; watch for repeat deals of this size as the leading indicator of post-credit offtake depth.
insights.quote: Google and Xcel Energy’s 1.9 GW portfolio deal, announced in Q1 2026, reflects the scale of data centre-driven procurement.
insights.locator: The changing market is also apparent in offtake

insights.claim: As some US utility wind procurement slows, corporate buyers could take a growing role in supporting new wind capacity while US electricity demand rises.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Signals a handover of offtake risk from regulated utility RFPs to corporate credit, changing the counterparty mix and financing terms for new wind projects.
insights.locator: As some utility wind procurement slows

insights.claim: More than 2,900 square kilometres of US offshore wind leases entered termination settlements during the first half of 2026, with proceeds from a $2.7 billion federal buyout expected to be redirected towards conventional energy, geothermal and fossil fuel projects.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Quantifies the structural shrinkage of the US offshore pipeline and a $2.7bn capital rotation out of offshore wind into conventional and geothermal supply chains.
insights.quote: More than 2,900 square kilometres of offshore leases entered termination settlements during the first half of 2026, with proceeds from a $2.7 billion federal buyout expected to be redirected towards conventional energy, geothermal and fossil fuel projects.
insights.locator: What is happening in offshore wind?

insights.claim: US offshore wind will deliver an important near-term supply boost as its under-construction pipeline approaches completion, but the segment remains exposed to significant policy and commercial uncertainty once that backlog is exhausted.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Offshore contributions to the 2027 peak are backlog run-off, not a repeatable pipeline — do not extrapolate offshore volumes past project completion.
insights.locator: Offshore wind will provide an important near-term boost

themes.theme: Repowering as the post-2030 growth vector

insights.claim: Around 81 GW of US wind capacity will be at least 15 years old by 2035, concentrated in Texas, the Plains and the Midwest, creating a large repowering addressable market as tax credits phase out.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Sizes the post-2030 demand pool for turbine OEMs and service providers at ~81 GW of aged assets, with geographic concentration that favours ERCOT and SPP-exposed players.
insights.quote: Around 81 GW of wind capacity will be at least 15 years old by 2035, much of it in Texas, the Plains and the Midwest.

insights.claim: Replacing older US turbines with larger, more efficient machines can raise energy yields while reusing existing land rights, grid connections and permitting precedents, cutting costs and development timelines relative to greenfield wind projects.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Repowering bypasses the two binding constraints on greenfield wind — permitting and interconnection — so it is where post-credit returns are most defensible.
insights.locator: Replacing older turbines with larger, more efficient machines

insights.claim: Improved turbine technology and higher capacity factors can reduce US wind's reliance on tax incentives, while rising electricity demand could create more favourable revenue conditions across the sector.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: The bull case for post-2030 wind rests on merchant power prices and capacity factors rather than subsidy — track realised capacity factors and power price curves as the key variables.
insights.locator: Improved technology and higher capacity factors

insights.claim: The US wind market will go through a fairly long process of readjustment rather than hitting a simple cliff edge in 2030 when federal tax credits expire.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the consensus 2030 collapse narrative; a gradual glide path implies less severe terminal-value haircuts for wind developers and OEMs than a cliff assumption.
insights.quote: The US wind market is experiencing a fairly long process of readjustment but will not hit a simple cliff edge in 2030.
insights.locator: The US wind market is experiencing a fairly long process

insights.claim: Capturing the strongest post-tax-credit US wind opportunities will require an investment logic built on commercial fundamentals rather than tax equity, favouring projects with a clear route to early construction and operation alongside repowering.
insights.speaker: Kárys Prado
insights.so_what: Implies shrinking tax-equity intermediation volumes and a shift in wind financing towards merchant/PPA-backed structures — relevant for banks and infrastructure funds with tax-equity franchises.
insights.quote: Capitalising on them, however, will require an investment logic built on commercial fundamentals rather than tax equity.
